body.p:
Wāʼwalis lived at Bēʼtsǃᴇs. Bēʼtsǃᴇs is a pretty place. / At each end lived a chief of the tribe. At one end / was the house of Wāʼwalis. At the other end was the house of Mēʼqǃŭnts. / Wāʼwalis went sea hunting. When he went his son, G̣āʼtsidālał was crying. Then Wāʼwalis went spearing / and caught seals. He made a fire and/ singed [the seals]. He put stones on the fire, / butchered [the seals] and put the seal meat on the stones. Thus / overnight it remained on the stones. Then morning came the soul meat was done. He took it from the stones and put it into baskets. Then / he put into a separate one what his wife liked best. / His wife liked the hind feet best. Then he went. / He arrived at the house. Then he carried up the seal meat. / He took it from the canoe up the beach to his house. "Go on," said Wāʼwalis, "Call our tribe. Let them come and / eat what we got." Then his slave went. "Come, / tribe." They came into the house of Wāʼwalis. His tribe came in. / When all were in the house of Wāʼwalis they were given / seal meat and his tribe ate. He gave to his wife what she liked best. Then he finished. / The tribe went out. When it was new moon / the wife of Wāʼwalis went out. / The wife of Wāʼwalis was menstruating. / Then the wife of Wāʼwalis came back. Then the child of Wāʼwalis was crying. / G̣āʼtsidālał wanted to eat again. "Let us go spearing again," said he to / his slave. Then it was morning but they did not start. "This is a good / day, Wāʼwalis," he was told by his wife. "You lost this good
day, Wāʼwalis," he was told by his / wife. Then his slave would not go and he struck / his slave and the little one cried, "Why don't you strike your wife's lover? / Why do you strike me?" - "Don't say that, my dear," said Wāʼwalis. Then Wāʼwalis did not sleep at all. / In the morning they started. Now he was waiting for it to be night. Then he asked / his slave, "Who is my wife's lover, my dear?" - "G·īʼʟēᵋ / is your wife's lover." Then he went near and waited for it to be night. / Then he said he would go back. He went to the beach of his house and Wāʼwalis stepped out of the canoe. He went to the back of the house straight / to the head end of her bed. Then Wāʼwalis sat on the ground. / He listened to hear whether his wife would speak. He had not been sitting on the ground long / before his wife spoke with her lover. / His wife had G·īʼʟēᵋ, the son of Mēʼqǃŭnts for her lover. Mēʼqǃŭnts had four childrens. Then Wāʼwalis made a noise of gnawing. "Nnnn," said / his wife, "You bad one! Gnaw the heart of Wāʼwalis." / Wāʼwalis heard his wife say this. Then there was again the sound of speaking / of the wife of Wāʼwalis. Again he made a noise of gnawing. Then / the wife of Wāʼwalis spoke again. "Nnnn," she said again, "you bad one. Why don't you gnaw the heart of Wāʼwalis?" Then he waited again and again he / made a noise of gnawing. Now the wife of Wāʼwalis did not speak. / Again he made the noise of gnawing. Now his wife was asleep. / A gain he made a noise of gnawing. Now the wife of Wāʼwalis was sleeping. / He entered and came to the bed of his wife. He felt of his wife. Then his wife had her arm under the neck of her lover. / Then she and her lover were asleep. Wāʼwalis cut off the head of / his wife's lover. Then Wāʼwalis went out with the head of / his wife's lover. As soon as he had it he paddled away / in the night time. Then his wife awoke. Her child
cried very much. "What is the matter?" / "He soiled the bed." She carried out on her back / the headless body of her lover. She went to his summer seat and / laid the body down on the summer seat. He had for his summer seat a flat stone. She put it down in the summer seat as if he was basking in the sun. Now / the lover of Wāʼwalis wife had no head. In the morning Mēʼqǃŭnts made breakfast / and invited his tribe and the friends of his son / for breakfast. Then breakfast was ready. "Go to / your elder brother," thus the youngest brother was told. Then he started. "Awaken, G·īʼʟēᵋ breakfast is ready." / He did not awake. Then he was left by his youngest brother. / The youngest brother arrived at the house of his father. "He did not / wake up," said he. "Go again and take off his blanket / if he doesn't awake." Now he took off his blanket. Then his brother had no head. Then cried / the child. He cried as he was walking along to the house of his father, / " G·īʼʟēᵋ has no head!" said he. He came / to his father, Mēʼqǃŭnts. "Don't say that, my dear. How should your oldest brother be that way?" / said Mēʼqǃŭnts. They / started to look and indeed he had no head there in his summer seat. /

Wāʼwalis was away spearing seals. / Then the headless body was brought. "Go on, take [the body] aboard. Take it to the / head of the inlet called Wanuk. Never will die out these / many tribes. Even if they should disappear it will be good that they in number will be replaced, for / my dead son shall lie in a deep cave." They brought him / to the head of Wanuk.

Now Wāʼwalis had again obtained many seals. / Again he took them off the stones. They were cooked and Wāʼwalis took them out. / Then Wāʼwalis went home. He came in sight at the point of the village. Then Wāʼwalis paddled strongly. He raised his paddles high. He was seen by his tribe. "Do not raise
your paddles, Wāʼwalis. / The child of Mēʼqǃŭnts is gone." Wāʼwalis did not obey and raised / his paddles. He arrived at the beach and carried up / the seal meat and his seal meat was done. Then he arrived in his house. At once his slave walked through / the village and the whole tribe came into the house of / Wāʼwalis. They were given meat. His tribe ate / seal meat. Then he took up again his wife's basket. / In it was what his wife liked best. She took it out. "Is this what I like best?" thus the wife of Wāʼwalis would say. / "There is something else which you like best," he would say to his wife. Then / she arrived at the bottom and behold, there she saw the head of the dead lover / of Wāʼwalis' wife. "Ananaiʼ," said the wife of Wāʼwalis / when she saw the head of her dead lover. Wāʼwalis took what his wife liked best. Youl cry on account of what you like best," / said Wāʼwalis, and he struck his wife between the legs / with the head of her dead lover. He did not / strike his wife a long time before she was dead. As soon as she had been killed he went a board his canoe / when his wife had been killed and his tribe ran out of the house. Then Wāʼwalis cut up his wife. He cut out the heart of / his wife and hung the heart of his wife over the doorway. / He never believed her when she lied and said that / she was menstruating. Behold, whenever it is new moon / drops fall doon from the heart of his dead wife when it was hanging above the doorway / of the house of Wāʼwalis. Then he was pursued by his tribe. They tried / to attack the house of Wāʼwalis, but they could not enter / Wāʼwalis' house. Now they tried to do too much and his tribe left.

As soon as his tribe was reached / by the warriors he ran from his house starting away and going to the head of the place of Wāʼwalis. He did not see any person and he walked
up the river. / Then he tried to look around. There was no man to be seen. / He arrived at Ogwiwa and saw a small house. / There was no smoke in the small house. There was just one little house with smoke. He went there / and went to the door of the house at the end down river. He peeped in and there was nobody / in the house. He went out again and went to another / house. There was nobody sitting in the other house and / he went out again and again he peeped into another house. There was nobody sitting in the other house. / He went out again and peeped into another house. There was nobody / sitting in the house. He went out again and he peeped into another / house. Then he saw a little fire in the one house. He went in and / a great old man was lying on the floor on one side of a little fire. Не could not see. Behold, the great old man was blind. / The old man had the great name Wanuk. He was the only one in the house. / Then he spoke and questioned him, "Is my princess sitting / in her room here? Go on! go into the room of my princess / Xaᵋnyōʼs Xaᵋnyōʼsɛmēg̣a is the name of my princess." Wāʼwalis started and went into the room of Wanuk's princess. "What is the matter with / your tribe, Xaᵋnyōʼs?" / "My father's tribe has been killed off. / Inland from where we live the lake monster is the one who killed off / our tribe." "Does your father not see?" "No he cannot see." "Come, come out of your room / that I may cure your father. We are going to marry, Xaᵋnyōʼs." Then / Xaᵋnyōʼs came out. "Now cure my father and / we will marry." - "Do you know who I am? I am Wāʼwalis. / We shall be married. Now go on, let your
father turn his head this way that I may cure him with my water of life." Then Wanuk turned his face. Wanuk was the name of the great chief. Wāʼwalis blew / his water of life on him. He did so again and blew on his face. "Are you not / beginning to see?" - Yes indeed." Once more Wāʼwalis blew on him with his water of life. Then / Wanuk saw. He was able to see well. / "What has destroyed your tribe?" / - "The lake monster made the tribe disappear. It is there / inland." "Go and try to go to the beach, Xaᵋnyōʼsɛmēg̣a," said he, "that I may / try to kill it with my death bringer." He sent his wife and she started. His wife went ahead. His wife waded / in the water and the big lake monster opened its mouth. As soon as / it opened its mouth he turned over the death bringing end of his staff. Then / the sea monster opened and shut its mouth. Once more / he struck it with his death bringer. / Four times he struck it with his death bringer / and the big lake monster vomited out the tribe. The tribe came and lay heaped on the beach. / "Now gather together the / bones on the beach that I may try my / water of life." The bones of the tribe were gathered / and when all was ready Wāʼwalis sprinkled his water of life over them. Four times he sprinkled them with his water of life / and the tribe of his wife came to life. / The tribe of his wife raised their faces and they came to life. / Then they entered the houses. They were well and went from the beach / to the houses. "You will have us to work for you." Then / they were a big village and Xaᵋnyōʼs / the princess of Wanuk was married to Wāʼwalis.

It happened that the wife of Wāʼwalis went out at night. It was full / moon. Then the moon came down and carried away / the wife of Wāʼwalis. / Xaᵋnyōʼsɛmēg̣a was taken up. Then there was no way for Wāʼwalis to get back his wife. Then she was married to the / Moon. After four days Xaᵋnyōʼsɛmēg̣a was with child. / Quickly she gave birth to a / boy. Quickly acquired sense / the child of the moon. Then he made a plan that he would cry. He was crying. He made the plan because he wanted to come down to his grandfather. / Then the Moon made up his mind to take down his wife and / his child. Then Spider was called on account of / her rope. It was brought and they let / Xaᵋnyōʼsɛmēg̣a down. With abalone shells was set her blanket. She carried her / child. Then they were let down by the rope of / Spider. They came right down at / Red-Rocks. [The boy] was planning to have a sling. / Then he carried his sling. He came to the beach at the place Wanuk. Then he tried / to throw a sling stone. He threw across and made a hole / where his sling stone struck on the other side. Then he did the same again. He made a hole / where his sling stone struck the other side of Ăwīʼg·is. / That was the name of the toy. Now sling the child was named after / his own toy, the sling. Then he walked and he came to Ōʼbis. There were many birds. / Sling was standing on the beach. He threw a stone and they flew away. When he shot / birds fell down. "Someone is walking on the beach at Ōʼbis. He makes the birds fall down," said the tribe of his mother; / they made a stir about it. "It is he," said his tribe, "Go and look." They
went / to look what it might be. It was Xaᵋnyōʼs. / She came and entered the house of her father Wanuk. Then / Sling entered the house of his grandfather Wanuk.

He moved to another tribe and married among the tribe. / Wāʼwalis had a wife. He went hunting sea-otters / and Wāʼwalis came home. He came with a beautiful sea otter. / Then he skinned the sea otter and the fur was bloody. / He had several sea otters. Then he sent his wife. "Go and wash the fur of the sea otters. They are bloody." Then / his wife went. She went to the beach and carrled the sea otters on a rope. To the beach went / the wife of Wāʼwalis. She put her sea otters into the water. She was going to wash them / at the beach in front of the house. Then she went into the water. Then / his wife went up the beach to urinate. She urinated a long time. Then what she was going to wash was floating away and what she was going to wash drifted out. / Then her urine was at an end. "Go out to what you are washing," / she was told by several of her tribe. / Wāʼwalis' wife started and waded into the water. When she waded into the water / a killer whale came up outside of the sea otter skins. Wāʼwalis' wife was wading, as the sea otter skins drifted seaward / she waded after them. Again the killer whale came up. / Then he took the wife of Wāʼwalis. She was sitting on his back / in front of the dorsal fin of the killer whale. / He started and went out to sea with her. Then Wāʼwalis was told, "Wāʼwalis, your wife has been taken away." - "Who took her away?" / said Wāʼwalis. "The Killer Whale took your wife. / Wāʼwalis went. He was going after his wife. / Wāʼwalis went to the beach and he just lifted the sea on the land side. He went under the water and walked along under the sea. He reached the Crow and asked her, "Did you not see/ my wife?" - "Go on run, he just passed with your wife." Then
Wāʼwalis went along. He came to the halibut / and he asked him also, "Did you not see my wife?" / - "Go on, run Wāʼwalis. He just passed along with your wife." / Then he ran on again. He reached the codfish. "Did you not see my wife?" - "Run along. He just / passed with your wife." Thus he was told again. Then he came to the house of the Killer Whale. He went near the house of / the Killer Whale. Then Wāʼwalis saw that one was getting firewood. / He went to the place where Big-Belly was wedging. Behold it was be, the attendant of the chief of the Killer Whales. Then / Wāʼwalis bit off the point of the wedge of the wedger. Then he cried, / "Heēʼ, I am going to be scolded. He will be angry with me, the Big-Belly chief." / Then Wāʼwalis came out. He had been inside what was being wedged by / the fuel cutter. Then he asked him, "Why are you crying?" - "I have spoiled the wedge of the great chief." - "For whom are you getting firewood?" - / "For the chief of the Killer Whales." "Have you not seen my / wife?" "She is the one for whom I am making the fire." "Give me / your wedge," said Wāʼwalis. It was given to him. / Then Wāʼwalis put the wedge into his mouth, and he made the wedge whole again. "Now I am going to help you, if you should try to get your wife. / I shall be asked at once to start a fire, as soon as I / arrive with this my firewood. Then I shall make a fire / and when I have finished making a fire I am going to be sent to bring water. / Then follow me. Just stand in the doorway. As soon as I shall go to the fire in the house of the chief I shall / fall down and I will pour the water into the fire in the house. Then run, / take up your wife. Then pass me and / my spines will grow up. They cannot pass me in the doorway / of the house of the chief. Then you can get away with your wife." /

He was waiting for his children. He had four children who had sense. / The youngest one was G̣āʼtsidāʼlał. His children walked / along. They were waiting for / their father. They were walking along in the woods. They walked about without caring where they went. Then they came to a river. Then they cried on account of the / youngest one. "How can we get across? Yeē. How may G̣āʼtsidāʼlał get across?" / - "Why should I not get across? Can I not jump across?" / Then the oldest one jumped across. Then the four girls jumped across. / Then they were all across the river. They walked along again. Again they walked a long distance. Again they reached / a river. It was a little wider. Then they said the same as before. / Again they cried. The reason for this was their youngest sister. / "Can I not jump across?" Then they all jumped across again. / Then they were walking along again. Again they walked and came again to a river. Again they were in trouble, in case their / youngest sister had no way to go across. Then they jumped across again / and they were all across again. Again they went and they came to / a large river. The river was very large. Then / they began to cry. They cried, "Heēʼ. How shall G̣āʼtsidāʼlał get across. The eldest one went across. She climbed / a tree on the other side of the big river. She threw down a tree / on the other side of the river. Then the tree lay across / the other side of the big river. The younger sisters stepped on it / and they all came across. Thus they passed four rivers and again they walked along. Then they heard the noise of making a canoe. They walked along / and came near, going to the place where the canoe was being made. Then they saw / a woman making a canoe. They arrived in the woods where the canoe was being made. Behold, it was a big woman. / The child of the canoe maker was in the cradle. Then they arrived and G̣āʼtsidāʼlał pinched the legs /
of the child. "Don't do that G̣āʼtsidāʼlał, else it will cry." / She took her breast and threw her big breast back. / It reached the child. Then the child finished sucking. / G̣āʼtsidāʼlał pinched it again. "Don't do that, G̣āʼtsidāʼlał," she said, although she did not look. She was the big Adzi. / Then she did it again. She pinched it strongly. / "Don't do that, G̣āʼtsidāʼlał. It shall be yours." Then she did so again. / She pinched it again. Again she pinched it strongly. / "Ah-ah-ah-ah-ah," said the little child. "Do not do that G̣āʼtsidāʼlał. This canoe which I am making shall be yours." Almost finished / was the canoe that the woman was making. "Wi!" cried on each side the big canoe / that the woman was making. Young sawbill ducks were sitting on each side of the big canoe she was making. / Their mother was sitting in the bow. The mother of the young sawbill ducks was making a Chinook canoe. / Feathers were between the young sawbill ducks. They were sticking on the sides between the young sawbill ducks. They were sticking on "their heads. / Between the young sawbill ducks were spirits [?]. / Then she did so again. She pinched the hand of the / child. "Do not do that, G̣āʼtsidāʼlał. Yours shall be / my big apron. My big apron is a fire maker. My big apron burns up everything. So go ahead to your canoe. G̣āʼtsidāʼlał." / The she said, "Go ahead," and indeed the future canoe of G̣āʼtsidāʼlał started on the ground. / Speaking-Sides was the name of her canoe. "You will just sit down in the bottom. / Just say to your canoe, 'Go ahead,' G̣āʼtsidāʼlał." She launched it / and G̣āʼtsidāʼlał went aboard. She tried to say, "Go ahead," and the canoe paddled and started on the water. It began to move. / She said, "Go on, paddle," and nobody was seen. Then there was a noise of many people who said, "Go on," and the big canoe went along on the water. It returned / and went where it had started from. She instructed her again.

"I shall make war. I shall go and fight those who made war against Wāʼwalis." / - "Go on, dress your eldest sister. Now / you will try on her the mother of the young sawbill ducks." Then the eldest one was dressed / with the mother of the young sea birds. Then it did not fit her. Then her place was taken by her younger sister. They put on her again the mother of / the young sawbill ducks. Then she cut through the water and fluttered. It almost / seemed right. Then they changed again and again they put it on [the next younger one]. / Then she cut through the water. It almost fitted her, / when she cut through the water. Then her place was taken again by the youngest one. G̣āʼtsidāʼlał was dressed. Then she cut through the water and she also fluttered. / She imitated the young sawbill ducks rightly. Now the last one / did rightly. Now they agreed that she did rightly. At last she did rightly [?]. Then she was instructed / by the big Adzi what she should do to those against whom she was going to make war to take revenge. / She was going to make war against those who had been married to her father. Then she arrived on the other side of the point of the village. Then she put on the / mother of young sea birds and she went into the water in front of the / big village. She used as a decoy the young sawbill ducks. / She came out at the point of the big village. Then she swam through the water. They saw her / and a great noise was made, the noise of canoes being put into the water by the great tribe. They were all on the water in their canoes. Then the young sawbill ducks turned back. / They turned and paddled after them. All went out to sea. / They came paddling. Then she said, "Go ahead, Big-Canoe-That-Says-'Wi', / paddle." No one was seen paddling on either side of the big canoe. The young sawbill ducks went through the water but it was only G̣āʼtsidāʼlał dressed as the mother of the young sawbill ducks. / Then they all gathered on the
water. She took up in the canoe the apron. Then she struck out with it. She struck out with her fire making apron. Then / they caught fire and all those who paddled after the young sawbill ducks were burned. Then she threw it upward. They arrived at the village. Behold / Wāʼwalis had come back. Behold he had returned. [He] had gone after his wife. Then the whole village was burned. /
